decks.title: Society, Law and Ethics — Part 1: Digital Footprints, Etiquette, Privacy and Intellectual Property
goals: Distinguish active and passive digital footprints and describe the behaviour of a responsible netizen
Explain data protection, privacy and safe online behaviour
Describe copyright, patent and trademark, their violations, and open source and Creative Commons licences

slides.heading: Society, Law and Ethics
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **behaving well online** and **respecting other people's work**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: digital footprints, netizens and etiquette, data protection, intellectual property, and open source software with licences
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every time we use a phone or a computer we join a digital society. In this part we look at the trail we leave online, how a responsible netizen behaves, how to protect our data, and how the law and licences protect the work of creators.

slides.heading: Digital footprints
slides.body_md: Every online action leaves a **digital footprint**: the trail of data about a person.

rows: The user knowingly submits the data
Posts, comments, e-mails sent, forms filled in
Data is collected without the user acting
IP address, browsing history from cookies, device details, location data

visual.alt: Table comparing active and passive digital footprints: how each is made and examples of each
visual.caption: Active means submitted on purpose; passive means collected in the background.

slides.narration: A digital footprint is the trail of data you leave online. The active footprint is what you knowingly submit, such as posts, comments and e-mails you send. The passive footprint is collected without you doing anything, such as your address on the network, browsing history from cookies, and device details.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: active or passive?
slides.body_md: Decide for each action whether the user **submitted** the data on purpose.

rows: Sends an e-mail to a teacher
A website logs the IP address of a visit
Uploads a video to a class channel
Browser cookies note the pages viewed
Types her name in an online quiz form

visual.alt: Table that classifies five online actions as active or passive digital footprints
visual.caption: Ask: did the user submit it on purpose?

slides.narration: Ask one question: did the user submit this data on purpose? Sending an e-mail, uploading a video and typing a name into a form are all deliberate, so they are active. A site noting the visit address and cookies recording pages viewed happen in the background, so they are passive.

slides.heading: Quick check: kinds of footprint
slides.body_md: Fill in the blank.
slides.narration: Remember what makes a footprint active.

slides.heading: Digital society and netizens
slides.body_md: A **netizen** is a member of the online community, with **rights** and matching **responsibilities**.

rows: Respect the privacy of other people
Express views politely, without hurting others
Protect your own data and other people's data

visual.alt: Table pairing each right of a netizen with a matching responsibility: access to information with checking facts, privacy with respecting others, freedom of expression with politeness, and safety with protecting data

slides.narration: Netizen joins the words net and citizen. A netizen has rights, such as access to information and privacy, and each right comes with a responsibility. We check facts before sharing, respect the privacy of others, express views politely, and protect data, our own and other people's.

slides.heading: Net, communication and social media etiquette
slides.body_md: **Netiquette** is the set of accepted rules of polite behaviour online.

rows: Respect others, follow the rules of the site
Rude or hurtful behaviour, spreading rumours
Clear subject, polite words, reply in time
Capital-letter shouting, abusive words, long messages without need
Think before posting, ask before sharing others' photos, credit sources

visual.alt: Table of three areas of etiquette, net, communication and social media, with what to do and what to avoid in each

slides.narration: Netiquette means polite and responsible behaviour online. In e-mail and chat, use a clear subject and polite words, and avoid shouting in capital letters. On social media, think before posting, ask before sharing someone else's photo, and do not spread unverified news.

slides.heading: Data protection and privacy
slides.body_md: **Data privacy** is control over how personal information is collected, used and shared.

rows: Never share; use strong passwords and two-step verification
Strangers can trace or impersonate you
Use privacy settings; ask before sharing others
Shows where you are or will be
Switch off location sharing for apps that do not need it

visual.alt: Table of kinds of personal data, the risk if each is made public and how to protect it

slides.narration: Privacy means controlling who can see and use your personal information. Passwords and one time codes must never be shared. Birth date, address and school should stay out of public profiles. Use privacy settings for photos, and switch off location sharing where it is not needed.

slides.heading: Safe online behaviour
slides.body_md: Build a small **habit of checking** before every share.

visual.alt: Flow of a safe sharing habit: pause before you post, check the source, check who can see it, then share or keep it private
visual.caption: A short check before every share.

slides.narration: A short routine keeps you safe. Pause before you post. Check the source of what you are sharing. Check who can see it. Then either share it or keep it private. Remember that deleting a post later does not remove copies that others have saved.

slides.heading: Quick check: before sharing
slides.body_md: Put the steps in order.
slides.narration: Think about what comes first, checking the message or forwarding it.

slides.heading: Intellectual property rights
slides.body_md: **Intellectual property** is the creation of the mind; the law gives its creator rights over it.

rows: Original creative works, from the moment they are created
A novel, a song, a drawing, program code
A new, useful invention, for a limited period
A new design of a water filter
A name, logo or symbol that identifies the maker of goods or services
A biscuit maker's name and logo

visual.alt: Table of the three kinds of intellectual property right, copyright, patent and trademark, with what each protects and an example

slides.narration: Intellectual property means creations of the mind. Copyright protects original creative work such as books, songs and program code. A patent protects a new and useful invention for a limited period. A trademark protects the name, logo or symbol that tells buyers which maker a product comes from.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which right fits?
slides.body_md: Match the situation to **copyright**, **patent** or **trademark**.

rows: A student writes a poem for the school magazine
A team invents a low-cost seed-planting device
A tea shop chooses a distinctive logo for its cups
A programmer writes the code of a quiz game

visual.alt: Table matching four situations to copyright, patent or trademark
visual.caption: Creative work: copyright. Invention: patent. Identifier of goods: trademark.

slides.narration: Look at what is being protected. A poem and the code of a game are creative works, so copyright applies. A new device that solves a problem is an invention, so a patent fits. A logo that identifies a shop's goods is a trademark.

slides.heading: Violation of IPR
slides.body_md: Using protected work without permission or credit is a **violation**.

rows: Presenting another person's work or ideas as your own, without credit
Pasting an article into a project with no source named
Copying, sharing or selling a protected work without permission
Selling unauthorised copies of paid software
Using a mark that is identical or confusingly similar to another maker's mark
A stall copying the name and logo of a known brand

visual.alt: Table of the three violations of IPR: plagiarism, copyright infringement and trademark infringement, each with its meaning and an example

slides.narration: There are three common violations. Plagiarism is presenting another person's work or ideas as your own without credit. Copyright infringement is copying, sharing or selling a protected work without permission. Trademark infringement is using a mark that is identical or confusingly similar to another maker's mark.

slides.heading: Quick check: spot the violation
slides.body_md: Choose the correct term.
slides.narration: The student used another person's words without naming the source.

slides.heading: Proprietary and free and open source software
slides.body_md: In **free and open source software** the word free is about **freedom**, not price.

rows: Freedom to use, study, change and share (not always free of cost)
The community and the licence terms

visual.alt: Table comparing proprietary software with free and open source software in source code, changing and sharing, meaning of free, and control

slides.narration: Proprietary software is owned by a person or company, keeps its source code closed and limits copying and changing through its licence. Free and open source software makes the source code available and allows you to use, study, change and share it. Free here means freedom, and it need not mean zero cost.

slides.heading: Software licences: GPL and Apache
slides.body_md: A **licence** states what a user may do with software.

headers: If you share a changed version
rows: It must also be shared under the GPL, with its source code
You may share it under your own terms, even in a closed product, if you keep the notices and credit

visual.alt: Table comparing the GPL, a copyleft licence, with the Apache licence, a permissive licence, in what must happen when a changed version is shared
visual.caption: Copyleft passes the freedoms on; permissive licences ask for little.

slides.narration: A licence tells users what they may do. The GPL is a copyleft licence: if you share a changed version, you must share it under the same licence with its source code. The Apache licence is permissive: you may use the code even inside a closed product, if you keep the notices and give credit.

slides.heading: Creative Commons licences
slides.body_md: Creative Commons lets creators allow some uses of their **creative work** in advance.

headers: What it asks of the user
rows: Release new versions under the same licence
Do not use the work for commercial gain

visual.alt: Table of the four Creative Commons elements BY, SA, NC and ND with their names and what each asks of the user
visual.caption: Elements are combined to make a licence, such as BY-NC.

slides.narration: Creative Commons licences are built from four elements. BY asks users to credit the creator. SA, share alike, asks that new versions carry the same licence. NC, non commercial, forbids use for profit. ND, no derivatives, allows only unchanged copies. They are meant for creative works more than for software.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: reading a licence
slides.body_md: Read two licence codes: **BY-NC-SA** and **BY-ND**.

rows: May you use it for profit?
Yes, if the work is not changed
May you edit or remix it?

visual.alt: Table that reads two Creative Commons licences, BY-NC-SA and BY-ND, answering whether credit is needed, whether profit use, editing and remixing are allowed, and the licence for a new version
visual.caption: BY-ND allows commercial use of unchanged copies because it has no NC element.

slides.narration: Take each element in turn. With BY, NC and SA you must credit the creator, you may not use it for profit, you may remix it, and your new version must carry the same licence. With BY and ND you must credit, you may not change it, but unchanged copies may be used even commercially.

slides.heading: Quick check: Creative Commons
slides.body_md: Match each element with its meaning.
slides.narration: Recall what each of the four letter codes asks of the user.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: net, communication and social media: be polite, think before you post
guard passwords, OTPs, photos, location and personal details
copyright, patent, trademark; violations: plagiarism, infringement
proprietary, GPL, Apache, Creative Commons BY, SA, NC, ND

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: footprints, etiquette, privacy, intellectual property rights and licences

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Footprints are active or passive. A netizen follows etiquette and protects privacy. Copyright, patent and trademark protect creations, and plagiarism and infringement violate them. Software may be proprietary or open source, and licences such as the GPL, Apache and Creative Commons state what users may do.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give **one example** with each footprint, right or violation you define.
Name the **right that fits** a situation: creative work, invention or identifier.
Remember that **free** in open source means freedom, not zero price.
Explain each Creative Commons element by what it **asks of the user**.
State copyleft (GPL) and permissive (Apache) as **different rules for shared changes**.
slides.narration: Some advice for the exam. Give an example with every definition. When a situation is described, name the right that fits. Remember that free in open source means freedom. Explain each Creative Commons element by what it asks of the user, and keep the GPL and Apache licences apart.

decks.title: Society, Law and Ethics — Part 2: Cyber Crime, the IT Act, E-waste and Technology in Society
goals: Identify cyber crimes and the kinds of malware, and describe safe browsing, identity protection and confidentiality
State the purpose and scope of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (amended 2008)
Explain e-waste management, health effects of technology use, and gender and disability issues

slides.heading: Cyber crime, the law and technology in society
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **threats**, **protection** and **responsible use of technology**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: cyber crimes, malware, cyber safety, the Information Technology Act, and e-waste, health and inclusion
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we meet the common cyber crimes and the malware behind many of them, learn how to stay safe, and see how the Information Technology Act deals with cyber offences. We end with the effects of technology on the environment, on health and on fairness in society.

slides.heading: Cyber crimes at a glance
slides.body_md: A **cyber crime** is an offence in which a computer, a network or data is the target or the tool.

rows: Unauthorised entry into a computer system or account
Secretly capturing data while it travels over a network
Fake messages that trick people into giving details or money
Files are locked until a payment is made
Offensive or repeated hurtful messages aimed at people

visual.alt: Table of cyber crimes and what happens in each: hacking, eavesdropping, phishing and fraud e-mails, ransomware, and cyber trolling and bullying

slides.narration: Cyber crime is an offence carried out using computers or networks. Hacking is unauthorised entry. Eavesdropping is secretly capturing data in transit. Phishing and fraud e-mails trick people. Ransomware locks files for payment. Trolling and bullying hurt people with offensive or repeated messages.

slides.heading: Hacking and eavesdropping
slides.body_md: Hacking is a crime when it is done **without permission**.

rows: Find weaknesses so they can be fixed
Lawful, when within the agreed limits

visual.alt: Table comparing an ethical hacker with a malicious hacker on permission, purpose and legal position

slides.narration: Hacking means gaining access to a system. An ethical hacker has the owner's permission and tests a system to find weaknesses so that they can be fixed. A malicious hacker has no permission and steals, damages or misuses data. Eavesdropping secretly captures data as it travels, for example on an open Wi-Fi network.

slides.heading: Phishing and fraud e-mails
slides.body_md: **Phishing** is a fake message or page that imitates a trusted sender to steal details.

rows: Sender address with a small spelling change
Threat or deadline: account closes today
Request for password, OTP or card details
A genuine bank never asks for these by message
It may lead to a copy of the real page
Prize you never entered for, with a fee to claim it
Fraud e-mails promise money to collect yours

visual.alt: Table of warning signs of phishing and fraud e-mails with the reason why each is suspicious

slides.narration: Phishing uses a fake message or page that imitates a trusted sender. Watch for an address with a small spelling change, a threat or deadline, a request for a password or one time code, or a strange link. Fraud e-mails also promise prizes and ask for a fee.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: spotting the signs
slides.body_md: A message from a shop says you won a prize and must pay a small fee today.

rows: The sender address misspells the shop's name
It says you must pay a small fee to claim a prize
A fraud e-mail asking for money
It tells you to act within the hour
It asks for your card number and OTP
Genuine firms do not ask for these in messages

visual.alt: Table of four clues in a suspicious e-mail and what each one tells us
visual.caption: Several clues together make the case.

slides.narration: Read the message clue by clue. The misspelt sender address shows imitation. The fee to claim a prize is a fraud. The demand to act within the hour is false urgency. A request for your card number and code is something genuine firms never make by message. Do not reply, and report it.

slides.heading: Quick check: which malware?
slides.body_md: Choose the correct term.
slides.narration: Files are locked and a payment is demanded.

slides.heading: Ransomware, cyber trolls and cyber bullying
slides.body_md: Some cyber crimes hurt **files**, others hurt **people**.

rows: Malware that locks files and demands payment
Keep offline backups; do not open unknown attachments
Posts provocative or offensive messages to upset or start fights
Do not feed it; block and report
Repeated online harassment of a person
Save the evidence, block, tell a trusted adult, report

visual.alt: Table of ransomware, cyber trolls and cyber bullying with what each is and a sensible response

slides.narration: Ransomware holds files hostage, so keep backups away from the computer. A cyber troll posts provocative or offensive messages to upset people, so do not feed it, block and report. Cyber bullying is repeated online harassment, so save the evidence, block the sender and tell a trusted adult.

slides.heading: Malware
slides.body_md: **Malware** is harmful software. Know how each kind behaves.

rows: Attaches to files and spreads when they are run or shared
Copies itself across a network on its own, needing no host file
Looks like useful software but hides harmful actions
Shows unwanted advertisements, often as pop-ups
Secretly watches what you do and reports it

visual.alt: Table of kinds of malware, virus, worm, Trojan, adware and spyware, and how each behaves

slides.narration: Malware means harmful software. A virus attaches to files and spreads when they are run or shared. A worm copies itself across a network on its own. A Trojan hides harm inside a useful looking program. Adware shows unwanted advertisements, and spyware secretly watches and reports what you do.

slides.heading: Quick check: kinds of malware
slides.body_md: Match each malware with its behaviour.
slides.narration: Think about which one needs a host file and which one travels by itself.

slides.heading: Cyber safety
slides.body_md: Three ideas keep a user safe: **safe browsing**, **identity protection** and **confidentiality**.

rows: Visiting sites and downloading files with care
Check the address and secure connection; download from trusted sources; keep antivirus updated
Keeping your identity from being misused
Never share passwords, OTPs or ID numbers; use two-step verification
Information is seen only by authorised people
Use privacy settings; share personal data only when needed

visual.alt: Table of cyber safety ideas, safe browsing, identity protection and confidentiality, with the meaning and habits for each

slides.narration: Safe browsing means checking the address and the secure connection, and downloading only from trusted places. Identity protection means never sharing passwords, one time codes or identity numbers. Confidentiality means information is seen only by those who are authorised, which we support with privacy settings.

slides.heading: Quick check: is antivirus enough?
slides.body_md: True or false?
slides.narration: Think about whether software alone can stop a user from being tricked.

slides.heading: The Information Technology Act, 2000
slides.body_md: India's **IT Act, 2000** (amended in 2008) gives a legal frame for electronic transactions and cyber offences.

rows: Electronic records and digital signatures are valid in law
Certain misuse of computers and data is defined as an offence
Offences can be punished or compensated
Disputes are decided by officers, with appeal to a tribunal such as the Cyber Appellate Tribunal

visual.alt: Table of the purposes of the Information Technology Act 2000 as amended in 2008: legal recognition, cyber offences, penalties, and adjudication and appeal
visual.caption: The Act is described here by purpose; section numbers are not needed.

slides.narration: The Information Technology Act of two thousand, amended in two thousand eight, has several purposes. It gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures. It defines cyber offences and penalties. And it provides adjudication of disputes, with appeals to an appellate tribunal.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which purpose applies?
slides.body_md: Link each situation to a **purpose** of the Act.

headers: Purpose of the IT Act involved
rows: A supplier accepts an order signed with a digital signature
Someone enters a company's system without permission
A dispute about such an offence is decided by an officer, then appealed

visual.alt: Table matching three situations to the purpose of the IT Act that applies

slides.narration: A supplier accepting an order signed with a digital signature shows legal recognition of electronic records. Someone entering a company system without permission is a cyber offence. A dispute decided by an officer, then appealed, is adjudication and appeal. We describe the Act by purpose and not by section number.

slides.heading: E-waste: hazards and management
slides.body_md: **E-waste** is discarded electrical and electronic equipment. Burning or dumping it is **harmful**.

visual.alt: Flow of e-waste management in order of preference: reduce, reuse, recycle through authorised recyclers, and safe disposal of what is left
visual.caption: Prefer the steps on the left.

slides.narration: E-waste is discarded electronic equipment such as old computers and phones. It contains toxic substances, so burning it pollutes the air and dumping it can contaminate soil and water. Manage it by reducing purchases, reusing devices, and recycling through authorised recyclers.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a school lab clear-out
slides.body_md: A lab has **48** old computers. 18 go to a village library and 20 to an authorised recycler. How many are left?

headers: What happens to the old computers

visual.alt: Table that splits 48 old lab computers into 18 given away, 20 recycled and 10 kept for spare parts, with shares of the total
visual.caption: The three parts add up to the whole.

slides.narration: The lab has 48 old computers. 18 working ones are reused, which is the first choice. 20 beyond repair go to an authorised recycler. The remaining 10 are kept as spare parts. The three parts add up to the whole, and nothing is burnt or dumped.

slides.heading: Quick check: the three Rs
slides.body_md: Fill in the blank.
slides.narration: Recall the middle word between reduce and recycle.

slides.heading: Health and technology
slides.body_md: Heavy use of screens can affect the **eyes**, **muscles**, **posture** and **habits**.

rows: Regular breaks; look at distant objects
Long typing or mouse use with poor wrist position
Poor sitting posture, screen too low
Supported back, screen at eye level
Overuse that replaces sleep, study and meals
Time limits, offline hobbies, talk to a trusted adult

visual.alt: Table of health problems linked to technology, digital eye strain, repetitive strain injury, back and neck pain, and internet addiction, with the cause and remedy for each

slides.narration: Long use of devices can cause digital eye strain, repetitive strain injury in the wrists and fingers, and back and neck pain from poor posture. Overuse can also become internet addiction. Take breaks, set up a comfortable position, and keep time for sleep, study and play.

slides.heading: Technology and society: gender and disability
slides.body_md: Technology should be **open to all**, whatever their gender or ability.

rows: Girls discouraged from computer or robotics clubs
Equal chances, role models, challenge stereotypes
A blind student cannot read an image-only page
Screen readers, alternative text, captions, keyboard access
A student has no device or connection at home
Shared labs, loan devices, low-bandwidth content

visual.alt: Table of issues of gender and disability in using and teaching computers, with an example and a way forward for each

slides.narration: Technology should be open to everyone. Girls should get equal chances in computer clubs, and stereotypes must be challenged. Students with disabilities need accessible design, such as screen readers, alternative text and captions, which are examples of assistive technology. Access to devices must be fair too.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: hacking, eavesdropping, phishing, ransomware, trolling, bullying
recognition of records and signatures, offences, adjudication and appeal
reduce, reuse, recycle; breaks, posture, balance
equal access for all genders and abilities

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: cyber crimes, malware, cyber safety, the IT Act, e-waste and health, and inclusion

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. Cyber crimes include hacking, eavesdropping, phishing, ransomware, trolling and bullying. Malware includes viruses, worms, Trojans, adware and spyware. Safe browsing, identity protection and confidentiality reduce risk. The IT Act gives legal recognition, defines offences and provides adjudication. E-waste needs reduce, reuse and recycle, and technology must be healthy and inclusive.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name the crime from the **scenario clues**: fake sender, locked files, repeated messages.
Separate **virus** (needs a host file) from **worm** (spreads by itself) and **Trojan** (disguised).
Describe the IT Act by **purpose**; do not quote section numbers or penalties.
Never recommend burning or dumping e-waste: say **authorised recycler**.
Pair every health problem with a **remedy**.
slides.narration: Some advice for the exam. Read the clues in a scenario before you name the crime. Keep virus, worm and Trojan apart. Describe the IT Act by its purpose and do not quote section numbers. For e-waste always say authorised recycler, and give a remedy with every health problem.

A **digital footprint** is the trail of data a person leaves online. The **active** footprint is made of what the user submits on purpose: posts, comments, e-mails sent and forms filled in. The **passive** footprint is collected in the background: the IP address, browsing history gathered by cookies, device details and location data.

sections.heading: 2. Intellectual property rights and their violation
sections.body_md:
**Intellectual property** is a creation of the mind. The law gives its creator rights, of three main kinds:
- **Copyright** protects original creative works (writing, music, art, films, program code), and arises as soon as the work is created.
- **Patent** protects a new, useful invention for a limited period.
- **Trademark** protects a name, logo or symbol that identifies the maker of goods or services.

Violations: **plagiarism** (presenting another's work or ideas as your own without credit), **copyright infringement** (copying, sharing or selling a protected work without permission, as in software piracy) and **trademark infringement** (using an identical or confusingly similar mark). Quoting with credit, or writing in your own words and naming the source, avoids plagiarism.

sections.heading: 3. Open source software and licensing
sections.body_md:
**Proprietary software** is owned by a person or company, its source code is kept closed, and its licence limits copying, changing and sharing. In **free and open source software (FOSS)** the source code is open and users may use, study, change and share it; free means freedom, not necessarily no price.

A **licence** states what a user may do. The **GPL** is a copyleft licence: changed versions that are shared must carry the same licence and source code. The **Apache licence** is permissive: the code may be used, even in closed products, if notices and credit are kept.

**Creative Commons** licences let creators allow some uses of creative works in advance. The elements are **BY** (give credit), **SA** (ShareAlike: new versions under the same licence), **NC** (no commercial use) and **ND** (NoDerivatives: unchanged copies only). SA and ND cannot be combined, because SA concerns new versions and ND forbids them.

sections.heading: 4. Cyber crime, malware and cyber safety
sections.body_md:
**Hacking** is unauthorised access (an ethical hacker works with the owner's permission). **Eavesdropping** is secretly capturing data in transit. **Phishing** and **fraud e-mails** use fake messages to steal details or money; signs are a misspelt sender, urgency, requests for passwords or OTPs and strange links. **Ransomware** locks files for payment; offline backups are the remedy. A **cyber troll** posts provocative or offensive messages to upset people. **Cyber bullying** is repeated online harassment.

**Malware** is harmful software: a **virus** attaches to files and spreads when they are run or shared; a **worm** copies itself across a network on its own; a **Trojan** is disguised as useful software; **adware** shows unwanted advertisements; **spyware** secretly watches the user.

**Cyber safety:** safe browsing (check the address and secure connection, download from trusted places, keep antivirus updated), identity protection (never share passwords, OTPs or ID numbers) and confidentiality (information seen only by authorised people).

sections.heading: 5. The Information Technology Act, 2000
sections.body_md:
The **Information Technology Act, 2000** of India, amended in **2008**, gives a legal frame for the digital world. Its purposes are to give **legal recognition** to electronic records and digital signatures, so that online contracts and e-governance are valid; to define **cyber offences** such as unauthorised access and misuse of data and to provide for penalties; and to provide **adjudication** of disputes and **appeal** to a tribunal (the Act set up the Cyber Appellate Tribunal; since 2017 its work has been done by the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal).

For examinations, describe the Act by its purpose and scope. Section numbers, amounts of penalties and terms of punishment are not needed.

sections.heading: 6. E-waste, health and technology in society
sections.body_md:
**E-waste** is discarded electrical and electronic equipment. It holds toxic substances such as lead and mercury; burning it pollutes the air and dumping it can contaminate soil and water. Manage it by the **three Rs**: **reduce** purchases, **reuse** and repair devices, **recycle** through **authorised recyclers**.

**Health:** digital eye strain (breaks; look at far objects), repetitive strain injury (rest, stretch, natural wrist position), back and neck pain (supported back, screen at eye level) and internet addiction (time limits, offline hobbies).

**Technology and society:** girls and boys should have equal chances in computing; students with disabilities need accessible design and **assistive technology** (screen readers, captions, alternative text, speech input); fair access to devices matters too.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following creates an **active** digital footprint?

options.text_md: A website recording the type of device that was used to visit it
Writing and posting a comment on the school discussion board
A map app noting the places a phone has been to in the background
A search engine keeping a log of the pages that were opened from its results

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Writing and posting a comment on the school discussion board. An active footprint is left by what the user knowingly submits, such as a typed and posted comment. Device details, background location and search logs are collected without the user doing anything on purpose, so they are passive.

questions.stem_md: Kavya opens a stories website on her tablet without logging in or typing anything. Later she keeps seeing advertisements on other sites about the same stories. The data that made this possible belongs to her

options.text_md: active digital footprint
digital signature
public domain work
passive digital footprint

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** passive digital footprint. She submitted nothing herself; the site and its cookies gathered her visit details automatically. Data collected in this way without a deliberate action forms the passive part of a footprint.

questions.stem_md: A **netizen** is best described as

options.text_md: a member of the online community who has rights and responsibilities while using the internet
a government officer who decides which websites may be opened
a program that guards a network from outside attacks
a company that sells internet connections to homes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a member of the online community who has rights and responsibilities while using the internet. The word joins net and citizen: someone who takes part in online life and is expected to behave responsibly, just as a citizen does in society.

options.text_md: Trademark rules, since he has misused a brand name
Data protection rules, since he has shared a password
Communication etiquette, since capital letters read as shouting and the tone is rude
Licensing rules, since he has copied a program

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Communication etiquette, since capital letters read as shouting and the tone is rude. Courteous wording and a calm tone are the basics of communication etiquette. Nothing in the message concerns a brand, a password or a software licence.

post it only if she expects it to collect a lot of likes
ask the classmates for permission, and crop or leave out anyone who does not agree
post it with a line saying that anyone may copy it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ask the classmates for permission, and crop or leave out anyone who does not agree. Taking a photograph does not give permission to publish other people. Respecting consent, and the privacy of those who say no, is part of good social media behaviour.

questions.stem_md: Describe how a student who is a responsible netizen should behave online. Refer to communication etiquette, social media etiquette, digital footprint and data protection.
questions.solution_md: Marks are given for the four areas and a concluding link to responsible behaviour.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Communication etiquette:** use polite and clear language, avoid capital-letter shouting and abusive words, and reply promptly and respectfully.

**Social media etiquette:** think before posting, do not spread unverified news, take permission before sharing others' photos and report abuse instead of joining in.

**Data protection:** keep passwords and OTPs private, use strong unique passwords with two-step verification, and keep personal details out of public profiles.

**Patent** protects a new and useful invention and gives the inventor exclusive rights for a limited period. Making or selling the invention without the patent holder's permission violates the patent.

**Trademark** covers the name, logo or symbol by which buyers recognise who made the goods or services. Using an identical or confusingly similar mark to mislead buyers is **trademark infringement**, for example a shop copying a famous brand's name and logo.

questions.stem_md: A school wants to adopt a free timetable program, improve it and share the improved version with other schools. Compare proprietary software with free and open source software for this need, and explain how the GPL and Apache licences would differ for the improved version.

**GPL (copyleft):** if the school shares its improved version, it must also make the source available under the GPL, so every later user keeps the same freedoms.

**Apache (permissive):** the school may share the version under its own terms, even inside a closed product, provided it keeps the notices and gives credit.

answer.model_answer_md:
Cyber crimes cross borders and leave digital evidence, so ordinary rules about paper records were not enough; a specific law was needed.

The **IT Act, 2000 (amended 2008)** gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures, defines cyber offences with penalties, and provides adjudication and an appellate tribunal for disputes.

Law punishes offenders after the event, while these habits prevent the harm.

answer.model_answer_md:
**E-waste management:** first reduce purchases, then reuse and repair devices, and finally recycle through authorised recyclers; never burn or dump devices, because their toxic substances pollute air, soil and water.

**Eye strain:** tired, dry eyes after long screen use; take regular breaks and look at faraway objects.

**Repetitive strain injury:** wrist or finger pain from long typing and mouse use; take breaks, stretch and keep the wrists in a natural position.

**Poor posture or internet addiction:** neck and back pain from bad posture, or loss of sleep and routine through overuse; sit with a supported back and the screen at eye level, and fix time limits for use.
